To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the migration of photo-initiators from UV inks is negligible and that the migration of acrylates depends on the type of UV inks used.

(1) UV ink components (photo-initiators and acrylates) are present in food simulants after migration testing, and (2) their levels depend on the type of UV inks and the food simulants used in migration tests.

UV inks for primary food packaging contain photo-initiators and acrylate esters that can be detected in the headspace of the printed substrate and in food simulants (water, ethanol, olive oil) after a 24 h migration time at 40 °C, and that the levels of the migrating substances are in the range of 0.01–0.1 mg/kg of food simulant.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of potential migrating compounds and their quantification in the food simulants, and the assessment of the migration levels in relation to the food simulants.
the identification of chemicals in UV food packaging inks, and the development of analytical methods to quantify the levels in the ink layer.
the development of chromatographic methods to determine the levels of potential migrants in UV inks and the development of migration tests for food packaging materials printed with UV inks.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the levels of potential migrants from UV inks are very low and do not pose any risk to the consumer.
the UV inks tested in this study were not found to be a source of potential migration of chemicals into food simulants.
the migration tests of UV inks for primary food packaging are positive, i.e. there is no migration of any photo-initiator or acrylate.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
UV inks are safe and can be considered as an environmentally friendly alternative to traditional inks.
UV inks are a safe alternative to paste or liquid printing inks.
UV inks are not necessarily safer for food contact applications than the conventional ones.
The main takeaway from our work is that
UV inks intended as primary food packaging materials can be produced with a low potential for migration of photo-initiator molecules or acrylates.
the level of potential migrating substances from UV inks into food simulants is low, and in the case of acrylate monomer is negligible.
the level of photo-initiator in the ink layer is not a good indicator of the potential to migrate into the food simulant.
